newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Young Broadcasting stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Young Broadcasting stock tumbles.

text.p: Young Broadcasting Inc's stock tumbled Wednesday after an analyst said lagging advertising revenues at the company's Los Angeles television station could hurt its bottom line.
Young's stock was down 5 at 22-1/4, a 52-week low, by late afternoon. About 2.4 million shares changed hands, compared with a daily average of about 82,000.
Merrill Lynch analyst Jessica Reif said in a research report that national advertising at Young's KCAL-TV was expected to be weak during the first half of this year.

Reif expects her earnings estimate for Young to be reduced once the full-year impact was assessed. Currently, she estimates 1997 earnings at $0.40 a share. The consensus estimate among analysts is $0.39, according to First Call.
"We're surprised at the beating it's taking because (the current) numbers don't reflect it," said one analyst who asked not to be named, referring to the drop in Young's share price.
Still, the analyst said the issues raised in the Merrill Lynch report have prompted the question, "Is this the first of many surprises we're about to hear?"
A spokesman for Young did not immediately return a telephone call.

Young acquired KCAL last year from Walt Disney Co. Since taking over, the company cut the station's workforce to 235 employees from 354 and trimmed promotional spending. Young, which owns 12 television stations, is not involved in any other business.

Reif said she earlier expected a strong showing by KCAL would offset any decline in Young's third- and fourth-quarter advertising revenues compared with the same periods of 1996, when stations attracted considerable political advertising.

In addition, she said disappointing network ratings at ABC-TV, a unit of Disney, "continue to have an adverse impact on sales, particularly national spot sales." Six of Young's 12 stations are ABC affiliates.
In 1996, Young brought in about $11 million in net revenues from political advertising. The bulk of that arrived in the fourth quarter.
"The uncertainty is what's doing it," Reif told Reuters, referring to the stock drop. "Until we have a better handle on the numbers, no one likes uncertainty."
